utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, Elizabeth Spelman, Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with legal interns with Sara Butkovic and Raila Abas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we note for the record that Mr. Hadzic is not present and we received the waiver that has been filed. Before we call the expert, Dr. Seute, the Chamber would like to put on the table again whether we should go into private session. The Chamber is of the view that yesterday nothing has been revealed that is not already in the public due to the Defence's decision to make public the elements of Mr. Hadzic's health condition. There is no indication that today's hearing would be any different. Therefore, there seems to be little or no reason for private session today, as well as yesterday. Mr. Zivanovic, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, yesterday I just conveyed the information I've got after consultation with Mr. Hadzic and he didn't change his mind, but it is on you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Prosecution, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have no position on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we go into closed session for a moment, please -- or private session, rather. Just private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness, Dr. Seute, may be brought in. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I please ask you, for the record, to state your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tatjana Seute, November 15th, 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a neuro-oncologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Seute, you are about to make the solemn declaration by which all witnesses before this Tribunal commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you commit yourself to the -- you expose yourself, sorry, to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. So this being said, could I ask you to give the solemn declaration. The text of it will be given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Seute.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My name is Douglas Stringer and I'm an attorney for the Prosecution here at the Tribunal, and I've got some questions about the report that you've prepared on the basis of the Chamber's request. Do you have the report with you?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the course of my questions, if there is anything that you don't understand or that you wish me to be clearer on, please don't hesitate to let me know.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Seute, your background, as I understand it you're a practicing neuro-oncologist.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Which means that, I guess, in layman's terms your job largely involves treating people, patients who have conditions such as the one that has been the recent diagnosis for Mr. Goran Hadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's correct. I diagnose, treat, and guide patients with glioblastomas. That's my main job, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you examined Mr. Hadzic on the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And examination occurred closer to where you work at the UMC Utrecht, the hospital out in Utrecht?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The exam, according to your report, lasted about one and one quarter hours.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you've indicated in your report, actually, that in relation to one of the questions, you've never been to the Detention Unit --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you don't know what the conditions are out there in which Mr. Hadzic is currently being detained?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can see some of the papers you've got, and I know from its Scheduling Order, that the Chamber directed that you be provided with papers that have been submitted by the parties; the Prosecution and the Defence, in regard to sort of the legal question that's currently with the Chamber, which is to release Mr. Hadzic from the detention unit so he can go back to Serbia for the next few months until he comes back in May for his MRI evaluation.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you understand that that's the main issue that's before the Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Hadzic, did you discuss with him anything about the conditions, the place where he's proposing to go live in Serbia if he's released?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: We don't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about where he would go --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- if he was released?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before you examined Mr. Hadzic, you've indicated in your report that you reviewed all of the medical reports, the data, the images that were available to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think you had at least once conversation with Dr. Falke, whose the chief medical officer here at the --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- what we call the DU, the detention unit. And are you aware that the Chamber appointed another person to serve in your capacity - that is, as an independent expert?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: I was and I was aware and I also spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's Dr. Cras.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it you spoke to Dr. Cras, maybe just briefly, but just around the time that each of you submitted your reports?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you seen Dr. Cras's report?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you're aware, I take it also, that Mr. Hadzic, his treating physician is Dr. Martin Taphoorn.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he's based with the MCH, the hospital group here in The Hague. Is that --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he is like yourself a neuro-oncologist?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Taphoorn?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of Dr. Taphoorn and your review of the medical file for Mr. Hadzic, can you comment on the quality of the medical care that Mr. Hadzic has received so far in this case?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. The quality of the care Mr. Hadzic received until now is of very high quality. It's based on standard treatment decisions as we know until now in Europe and America and all over the world. Imaging is of excellent quality. Pathological reports are of excellent quality, and Professor Taphoorn is a highly respected oncologist in the neurological field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it Dr. Taphoorn is one of the people who developed or at least published what we've been referring to as the Stupp scheme which is sort of the regime of treatment that Mr. Hadzic is now undergoing?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah. It was a very large trial performed in the early end 1990s to 2000, 2005, a lot of neuro-oncologists put in their patients so that is why we are all there on the list of authors. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw your name on a number of publications as well, related to treatment of glioblastoma.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we actually move to the substance of your findings or your opinion, I did want to direct you to one part of the report and ask for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could go to page 4, which is the last page of your report, and the last paragraph there, and this is the answer to the question that is in the small Roman numeral (v). You said: "The median survival of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma multiforme varies from 12 to 14 months, however median indicates 50 per cent." And then the next sentence says: "The two year survival ranges from 25 to 30 per cent." So I wanted to ask you if you could clarify the 12 to 14 months there and whether that is accurate?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. It is accurate. You know, these numbers come, actually, from the Stupp trial, you know, this treatment, regimen Mr. Hadzic is receiving right now, is undergoing, is based on the Stupp trial. There were lots of patients in this trial, and if you look at the survival rates of these patients, you will get to a median survival close to 14 months. But if you -- because that's why I also took into account, I said from these numbers are based on trials and based on personal experience from our own hospital, because I run the biggest clinic in Holland. We have the largest amount of patients. Then you have to be -- no, you can have the number of 13.7 months. I took the number of 12 to 14 months because if you look at the at the whole of Holland, that will be the median survival. But to be very clear, for the patient in front of you, especially in this early phase of his disease, nothing is to be said about these 12 to 14 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I bring this to your attention because I think, again, for those of us who are not physicians or experts in your field, Dr. Cras --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- in his second report actually says that at present Mr. Hadzic's survival can be estimated in the range of 12 to 24 months.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- depending on the success of radio and chemo. So perhaps you can explain what is the -- what's behind the different ranges --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- that we're seeing here.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that what's behind if you look at the 12 to 14 months, that's -- that's the number that came out of the trial. All sorts of patients are in there, like, all the patients in bad physical condition even before starting, before diagnosed with the glioblastoma. There are patients who underwent surgery, like resection of the tumour. There are patients who didn't undergo surgery. There are patients with very large tumours in very eloquent sections of the brain. There are patients with very small tumours. All with the same diagnosis. So a very large scale of different sorts of patients. So if you look at the case, the patient as Mr. Hadzic, there is also in Dr. Cras's report, there are some elements that could be judged as beneficial prognostic factors like his relatively young age, although this disease is a disease of young people; his good physical condition; and then on the other hand, there are some factors that -- that are negatively -- negative prognostic factors like the multi- -- the fact that the tumour is in different parts of the brain so that a resection was not possible. If you add up all of these factors, then you can make little bit -- you can try -- let me clarify that. You can try to make little bit of a broad view. And then also Professor Taphoorn and Professor Cras think that it might be somewhere between 12 to 24 months. Personally, I think that in this part of his -- this stage of his disease, it's extremely difficult to say anything about his future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. When you examined Mr. Hadzic on the 11th of February, you indicated that although you did not perform any neuropsychological tests, you stated that he did appear to have no cognitive dysfunction?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Cras indicated in his report that he found Mr. Hadzic to be well-oriented, to express himself clearly --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- and that he tested normally on the Montreal Cognitive Exam.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question is whether Dr. Cras's findings and observations are generally consistent with your own on that?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they are generally consistent. I thought Mr. Hadzic was very clear minded. He answered my questions through the interpreter very quickly. Didn't need allot of time to think. Was orientated in time, space, and person. But -- well, as stated, I didn't do a real large battery of neuropsychological tests because that would take me like --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: -- hours to do that and I would have to involve my neuropsychologist and didn't go to that effort because I didn't think that it was necessary at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then getting to really the main point that you've been asked to address, if I could direct you to page 2 of your report. Actually, we're going to look at a couple of questions. And this is question number 2. And your -- here you're asked whether Mr. Hadzic will have the capacity to physically attend and participate in trial proceedings for a period of four months either during or after treatment. And then in your answer that follows, you state that in your opinion he would not be able to participate for four months during treatment or during episodes with serious side effects.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before I come back to the question, if we could just turn the page and go to question 4, which also relates to the same issue. This was if Mr. Hadzic is incapable of physically attending proceedings at the Tribunal, would he have the capacity to participate via video conference link set up in the UN Detention Unit. Now, as one of the people who was involved in suggesting questions, I think we might have done a better job for you in distinguishing between "attending" or what maybe I'll use today as "being present at" versus "participation," and so I would like to distinguish between those if I may in the questions that follow. Because in your answer to this question that we've just read, you -- first of all, you indicate or you refer to your previous answer, and then you express concern about the burden of intensive questioning and also the length of the proceedings, that being several months.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Dr. Seute, if I could ask you, first of all, perhaps you could describe or indicate for us when you were responding here, what was in your mind when you were thinking of "participation"?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: In my mind, as a medical doctor, I was thinking of "participating" being here in the trial room, being aware of what was said in the trial room, and being able to answer questions as I am now. That was my perception of participating in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now setting aside participation, those three things that you've just described - as being present, his listening, and his answering questions - setting that aside and focusing strictly on his capacity or ability to be present which is the first one -- maybe the first two, to be present and to follow the proceedings, let's say that that's what means -- that's sort of how we will define being present. He's physically present in the courtroom, he'd be sitting over there on that back bench, or even being in his room at the detention unit watching the proceedings live on a video screen, even perhaps with the ability to direct or to contact his lawyers here in the courtroom in realtime. So if that's how we define being present, taking that aside, and I guess I'm going to digress for a quick second to talk about the treatment regime now that he's going to be undergoing for the coming months. And as I understand it, he's going to be looking at least two more 28-day cycles, each of which involves five days where he's actually taking the chemotherapy --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- drug, and that's followed by a 23-day period of recovery.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That is how one cycle runs.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your report you said that if Mr. Hadzic's blood counts will improve it may be possible for him to attend and participate in a hearing for a limited time per day. Setting aside again participation in answering of questions, are you saying that during, say, the 23-day periods of recovery, it may be possible for Mr. Hadzic to attend as we've defined it either by being present in the courtroom or following from the UN Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Obviously depending upon how he's affected by the side effects?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that's a crucial thing you are mentioning there. I think depending on whether or not he will experience side effects, I can only then -- let me rephrase: If you know how he will react to this chemo regimen, then you can make a medical fair judgement about whether he will be able to be present. We know now that from his first treatment phase with the combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy that he has a serious blood count drop. That's a serious side effect. The counts he had are not life threatening be if they go down more, they are. They are a serious threat to his life. Now this new phase or this second phase of treatment is the same chemotherapy and it's indeed five days, but it's a much higher dose. So he will pulse -- he will get a lot of chemotherapy at once and especially the first cycle, you will not know what's going to happen afterwards. At this point, I'm not informed also about his blood counts right now. So I'm not even sure as far as I know right now, whether he will be able to start these cycles. But let's assume he will. Then I think you can make a fair judgement during the first 23 days of rest how this will affect him, how this will affect his blood counts, and then you can judge whether he can be present. If his blood counts stay at normal level, if he doesn't experience nausea and vomiting, if he doesn't experience extreme fatigue, then he can be present here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: And if I may make --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: -- just one more adjustment to that. I can imagine that you think, well, the five days of chemotherapy are the worst, but the phase afterwards, the recovery phase, that's when the patients experience the side effects. Mostly not during the five days of taking the medication. The blood counts are lowest at day 21, that's when I assume Professor Taphoorn will also do a blood count. And then at day 28, that's when I assume he will decide whether the second cycle will take place, assuming the first one will take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, really, the possibilities in terms of Mr. Hadzic's ability to be present, aren't necessarily linked to whether he's taking his chemo on a given day or not?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's linked to more how he's feeling and what his blood count is?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now in terms of -- I don't know how much or how little you know about what a trial day is here or how the schedule runs. One question on that: If -- would the possibility of Mr. Hadzic's ability to be present, would it be increased if the Chamber -- the Trial Chamber and the judges showed flexibility in scheduling shorter trial days, for example, of a few hours, or having the trial take place at times of the day that are better suited to Mr. Hadzic's schedule? I saw in one of the reports that he's got some insomnia but he's sleeping more during the day. So would flexibility on those lines also contribute to his ability to be present?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would -- that would be helpful, although it's very hard to -- to predict now how he will react and what adjustments have to be made. If I may speak from my experience, with, like -- I've seen like over 900 patients now who received this treatment and I all guided them myself. I've now got staff doing that with me. Then, I have patients who are in good condition, good physical health, even do some working chores during this chemotherapy; on the other hand, there are other patients, also young and physically well-fit patients, who really need hours of extra sleep during the day. It's really not possible up front to predict how it's going to be for him. But both scenarios and everything between that are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. One last question. And given what you've said earlier about the prognosis --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- and also given that his condition and his treatment programme, as I understand it, will be re-evaluated in the early part of May --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- would it be correct to say that Mr. Hadzic's ability to be present in trial proceedings will diminish over time just in a -- as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's very hard to say now. As in a general rule, yes, because he has a progressive disease and the treatment is aimed to slow it down, to stop it at best. And as you can read in my report, sometimes we're very successful. That means that we also have long survivals, also patients who didn't have a resection. But it's a small group, very small. Most people benefit from this treatment, of course, otherwise we wouldn't give it, but in time -- and it's really not possible to say at this point in time in what time, but in time he will diminish. He will develop neurological dysfunction, he will develop cognitive dysfunction, that is a matter of time, but just the amount of time we have can't be predicted right now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Seute.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Dr. Seute. My name is Christopher Gosnell. I'm here for Mr. Hadzic. You say in your report in answer to question 4(b)(ii) -- well, actually, it's just 4 -- 4(b) -- well, in any event, it's on page 3, you say: "The expected consequences of the radiotherapy and the chemotherapy are low blood count, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, rare. On the mid-long cognitive dysfunction, ranging from mild problems with concentration to serious amnesia." Are you -- and I'm interested in the expression mid- --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- long cognitive dysfunction. Is there a distinction in your mind between mid-long dysfunction and some shorter dysfunction?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. As I -- it's hard to explain like without starting lecturing, but radiotherapy -- I'm referring here to the side effects that radiotherapy can give to a person. The radiotherapy Mr. Hadzic underwent is aimed, of course, at the areas in the brain where the tumour is -- where the tumour locations are, because there are multiple locations. When you -- when the radiotherapist makes his plan, he will aim the radiotherapy, as I said, at the tumour locations, but also healthy neurons, healthy brain cells will be involved in this radiotherapy scheme. This will not affect you directly. You will not notice that. When you're receiving the radiotherapy, you will be -- patients can complain of fatigue, but they will not suffer from concentration loss directly. Within a time, and that's where the mid-long is kind of fake, and I can't be more specific about it, but the mid-long is then months to years, the healthy neurons, the healthy brain cells that receive radiotherapy will diminish in function, and then you can start experiencing concentration loss. And if it's a serious case, you can have serious amnesia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But is it common that you have glioblastoma patients -- glioblastoma multiform, while they are undergoing their chemotherapy, who present no apparent cognitive dysfunctions but who nevertheless complain and in reality have significant deficits in terms of more complicated sustained intellectual tasks?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Do you mean during treatment or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: During treatment.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: In my experience, most patients do complain in some -- to some extent of cognitive dysfunction. Although, I must say again there is a very wide range of how that affects them in life. I also have a quite some patients, quite some percentage of patients who continue doing their job, also highly educated patients, and continue being fully active in social and working life. Very different -- very difficult to say something in general about it because it's also because, like I said before, patients with brain tumours have cancer but they also have a neurological disease very much dependent on where the tumour is located in the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it a different way: Would it be unusual for you or would you consider it unlikely if a patient were to tell you that they have significant difficulties maintaining a train of thought or maintaining concentration over a one- or a two hour time-period, but when you see them you see no apparent cognitive dysfunction?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: And the question is whether that would be unusual? I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Whether that would be something that you would suspect that what they were telling you wasn't true or that they didn't, in fact, have such difficulties maintaining a train of thought or concentrating for one hour or two hours?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Whether I expect them to -- to have that or to not to have that or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether you would find that unusual or outside of the bounds of what would be expected for someone with a glioblastoma while undergoing the chemotherapy?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Well, again, it would depend on the location of the tumour. If you got a tumour in the frontal lobes, I would really be surprised if there would be no -- if a patient would tell me, "I've got no problems with maintaining thought" or "maintaining concentration over hours." If the tumour is in the occipital lobe, which is in the back of the head, that could probably be the case, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But in either way it would be quite possible or even probable in either of those cases that the person would complain exclusively about their ability to concentrate over a long period, digest information over that long period, engage in executive function over a long period, maintain short-term memory over a long period. Those wouldn't be unusual?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No, that wouldn't be unusual. In our hospital, if patients complained of that and there is a -- we have different neurological psychological tasks we perform on this patient, I would order a full neuropsychological exam to also examine the range of how long somebody can maintain concentration. You can just examine that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now in answer to question (a)(ii), you say: "In my opinion, Mr. Hadzic will not be able to participate in trial proceedings for four months during treatment and/or during episodes with serious side effects like low blood counts," and then you go on. And it was read by my learned friend opposite, so I won't repeat it except for the sentence after that where you say: "The near and median term future is very uncertain for him. His physical and neurological condition can change rapidly over time." Now, when you say "rapidly," do you mean to say that his condition could change from day-to-day to a significant degree?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible. But if I may explain a little bit how that can happen. At this time -- at this point of time, we -- or I are sort of clueless about in how the treatment is affecting Mr. Hadzic, how -- if the tumour is responding to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to make pauses between question and answer for the purpose of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think you can proceed, Dr. Seute.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So -- where were we. Oh, the rapidly -- rapidly change in his functioning. So at this time we don't know whether the treatment is effective. If we go to a worse-case scenario, then the treatment is not effective and tumour is growing inside his brain. You might say, well, we will notice that from the outside. He will have cognitive dysfunction or he will have neurological deficient or he will have another seizure. That doesn't have to happen. Mostly it doesn't even happen. Mostly what we notice is when the -- a tumour cell grows notice brain, then the healthy neurons will start swelling in the brain and brain edema will develop. That develops really rapidly and that's why patients can deteriorate in days. It's not the tumour growth itself that will be notable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in answer to my learned friend, you described that the consequences or side effects of the Temozolomide treatment can be felt -- in fact, is characteristically felt during the rest period, and that includes low blood platelets.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I don't know whether you've seen the medical report of the 18th of February, 2015, but the indication in that report is that: "The chemotherapy has had to be postponed due to a negative effect on the bone marrow leaving him with a serious platelet deficiency. He has shown a small recovery. The platelet numbers are increasing." Now as I understand it, the platelets were low enough that the chemotherapy was terminated on the 21st of January. So that means, as I understand it, that the platelets levels have been below the minimum between the 21st of January and the date of this report, the 18th of February. Now, is that a negative prognostic indicator about his ability to successfully undergo the rest of the chemotherapy and --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and can his anticipated life expectancy?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's hard to answer right now because if his -- if his platelets go up within a week, then I assume that Professor Taphoorn will continue giving him chemotherapy. And then, of course, you have to be really careful with, like, the dosage of the chemotherapy because you know Mr. Hadzic is prone to develop low platelets, have bone marrow suppression. But it's not necessarily that the -- that the next cycles will fail, you know. This can be a temporarily problem, and we've seen that patients are sometimes able to succeed six cycles of chemotherapy also with having these platelet drops in the first period. That is because this is a different regimen. You know, his first treatment was totally different -- different regimen with daily chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But this would be an example of what you were describing earlier; namely, the platelet levels decreasing at some period after the administration --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- or ingestion of the drug and having that effect continue for a considerable period. And in fact, here it seems it has spanned almost the entire recovery period of the first cycle.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to just ask you a couple of questions, and I'm not going to enlighten you about the specific details about what goes on in a trial here. But I would like to ask you about a more generic example that may be more familiar to you and to consider someone who is, for example, taking a seminar at the Utrecht University, and this seminar requires them to participate for a two-hour period and do, let's say, 200 pages of reading per class. And you have a person who comes to you with glioblastoma and they are taking the chemotherapy, and they say, "Doctor, I feel generally all right, but I cannot maintain my concentration sufficiently to do all of these readings and to be able to follow the class and occasionally to intervene." Now, can I first of all ask you would that be an unusual set of -- or description or self-reporting by the person of how they are able to function under these circumstances, and assume that the person has the profile of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No, that would not be unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, let's say the professor in the class decided that they didn't want to take the person's word for that, and they came to you and they said, "Dr. Seute, I don't believe that what this person is saying is true" or "maybe I believe what they are saying is true, but I'd nonetheless like to double-check and see precisely what is their performance level in relation to this seminar." Now, first of all, is there a test that you could or would administer to try to give some kind of a score or a measure in relation to that task? Is that possible, medically?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible medically. Actually, you could perform, again as I stated, a neuropsychological examination. That's an examination of a couple of hours, at least in our university hospital, and then you can address these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The Montreal Cognitive Assessment would be totally inappropriate for that; correct?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you also say in your report that -- and it's in respect of the questions I was asking you earlier about variability. And if this student came to you and said I am having this problem, how long would the tests -- or let's not say the student. Let's say the professor. How long would the test take to perform in order to achieve some kind of a score about this person's capacities?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: You mean how long would a neuropsychological examination take?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then is it possible that the person's capacities are varying from day-to-day?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, but well trained neuropsychologists take all that kind of information into account. Before making a report about the cognitive function, you also have to take into account the pre-illness level of a patient, and they are really trained to do that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it would certainly be possible for someone one day to have a certain level of mid- to long cognitive capacity which changes over the course of several days?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's also the case with healthy persons. If you're tired, your capacity to concentrate diminish. If for patients with neurological illness, irrespective of whether it's a tumour or a haemorrhage, this fluctuates through the day. Yeah. That's why I said it's very hard to predict for the long-term how it's going to be. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it's very difficult to measure over an extended period because it could change; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And it's very hard at this time to predict or to even say something about Mr. Hadzic because we don't even know, you know, what his status is at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you a few questions about prognosis.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you've confirmed today what you said in your report, that the median survival is 12 to 14 months. Is the starting point for that median the beginning of radiotherapy?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No, the starting point is the -- they had two different trials, because these are again trial numbers, trial figures. The starting point is the day the diagnosis was made by the pathologist, so the day of surgery, the day of biopsy. That's the starting date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you talked a little bit about progression in response to some questions by my learned friend. Do you know the median time to progression for students -- patients with glioblastoma, multiform?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Depends if you go to general, for the general population, so all sorts of patients are involved in this -- in this illness, so the older patients, the younger patients, then the median time to progression is around six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I think that the Stupp report that you referred to as a landmark, the median time to progression in that study where the median age was 56, the median time to progression was seven months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you agree that progression is usually, not always, but usually associated with a steep decline in physical and cognitive condition?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: I think it's too harsh to say "usually," and that is because in my experience, and I know that's also the way Professor Taphoorn works, we perform quite a lot of MRI scans once we started. Every three months we look at these patients. A lot of times we see progression on the scan before patients will experience complaints from that progression. And of course from -- taken from the point of the landmark study of Stupp, that's 2005, you know, a lot of -- fortunately, a lot of progress has been made, and we start second-line treatments, experimental treatments. So I would say regularly we see that patients decline after -- physically after progression of disease, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And cognitively?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Depending on the -- on the location of the tumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's not unusual that there is a decline in cognitive and physical condition around the --

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- time of progression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Seute, I have a few questions as well, and they might appear to you as repetitive but that is probably because we need a little bit more time to understand all these things that we are not used to handle. In your report, you have indicated that Mr. Hadzic will not be able to participate in trial proceedings during treatment and/or during episodes with serious side effects like low blood counts.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There are two elements here. During treatment, on the one hand; and on the other hand, during episodes with serious side effects like low blood counts. Am I correct in reading this as serious side effects, like low blood counts, can occur during the treatment days but they could also occur or continue during nontreatment days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And then I specifically refer to the blood count. They drop after the therapy is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday Dr. Cras told us that in general the side effects other than the blood count are related to the time of administration of the drug, so they occur shortly after administration but would probably last throughout the day. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: I would agree with that assessment if you refer to the nausea and vomiting. Vomiting is very rare with this kind of chemotherapy. However, the fatigue, which is explained by bone marrow suppression, you know, your body has to work hard to keep up your blood count, that patients experience that, well, yes, during treatment, but mostly after the treatment, and that's an experience that's not in the books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would come back now to that, to the blood count. And with regard to that problem, Dr. Cras explained to us yesterday that this side effect does not have an influence on the patient's physical status. The reduction of blood platelets, he told us, and reduction of white blood cells leads to an increased tendency to bleed and increased tendency to have an infection.

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You would agree?

utterances.speaker: TATJANA SEUTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However -- you know, let me explain differently: The fact that if I have a low blood count, you wouldn't see anything from the outside. If I were to fall, I wouldn't bleed to death. Nothing would happen. However, there's another mechanism there. Your bone marrow production, your blood cell production we all have, is making all of hours. And that's -- that's not what I'm thinking, that's not a hypothesis, that's what's going on in your body. Chemotherapy is directed to dividing cells. Tumour growth is dividing cells. It's nothing more, nothing else. Chemotherapy will go and try to address all cells in your body that are dividing. Well, as mature persons, of course, most organs don't have dividing cells any more, but the bone marrow, so that's where the blood cells are generated, has constantly dividing cells and your chemotherapy is trying to diminish that. So the production is going up anyway, and that's what the fatigue causes. Not the fact that the blood platelets are low, no, but the bone marrow production has to go up. However, the fatigue, if I may elaborate a little bit on that. It's, as I stated before, it's very much based on individuals. I mean, some person doesn't experience fatigue at all or only to a very, very small amount. Other persons have to rest for several hours during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there are no further questions from the parties, Dr. Seute, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness and the court usher will escort you out of the court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, the Chamber would like to put a few questions to the Defence with regard of their request for provisional release. First question is this: Who will serve as Mr. Hadzic's doctor in Novi Sad eventually? You should indicate -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a good idea, indeed, to go into closed session now -- private. Private session will be sufficient. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing sine die at 3.40 p.m.
